cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A diode can do more than redirect current.
Choose the right semiconductor, and electrical energy can become visible
light.
In a light emitting diode, or LED, forward bias injects carriers that can
recombine and emit photons.
Efficient light emission requires suitable materials; an ordinary silicon
diode
is not automatically a useful visible LED.
The approximate photon energy is related to the semiconductor energy gap,
although real emission has a spectrum and other device effects.
For a simple estimate, suppose the emitted photons have energy two electron
volts.
Using h c approximately twelve hundred forty electron volt nanometers, their
wavelength is about six hundred twenty nanometers.
Greater photon energy means shorter wavelength.
Now connect the LED safely in our classroom circuit model.
A five volt supply drives an LED whose assumed forward drop is two volts.
To target ten milliamperes, the resistor must drop the remaining three volts.
Divide three by zero point zero one amperes: choose three hundred ohms in this
idealized calculation.
A real component choice must account for tolerances and ratings.
Notice that we did not use zero point seven volts for the LED.
Different colors and materials have different forward characteristics.
Its I V curve has a steep forward branch; brightness generally responds to
current over a useful range, not to a universal voltage rule.
Pause and name the conversion: electrical energy in, light out.
That direction will help us distinguish the next two devices.
Now reverse the energy story.
A photodiode detects incoming light rather than producing it.
Absorbed photons can create electron hole pairs.
The junction field helps separate these carriers so they contribute to a
measurable current.
In the usual JEE detection arrangement, the photodiode is reverse biased.
Reverse bias widens the depletion region and can improve collection speed.
Photodiodes can also operate without external reverse bias, so reverse bias is
a common operating mode, not the only physically possible one.
Keep that qualification in mind.
Even without illumination there can be a small dark current.
Under suitable fixed wavelength and operating conditions, the added
photocurrent is approximately proportional to incident optical power.
For an original numerical example, assume responsivity is zero point four
amperes per watt.
Incident power is two milliwatts.
Multiply zero point four by zero point zero zero two watts to get zero point
zero zero zero eight amperes, or zero point eight milliamperes of
photocurrent.
If dark current is two microamperes and both contributions flow in the same
measured reverse direction, the current magnitude becomes about zero point
eight zero two milliamperes.
Check the sign convention before adding signed currents on a graph.
More light shifts the reverse current magnitude under the same conditions.
This example assumes the device is in its linear range.
The key contrast is easy: an LED sends light out under forward operation,
while
a photodiode turns incoming light into an electrical detection signal.
A solar cell also absorbs light, but its main job is delivering electrical
power to a load.
Illumination creates carriers, and the junction separates them, producing a
photovoltage and a current that can flow through an external circuit.
There is no external bias battery supplying the cell in its normal power
generating role.
A graph needs a clear convention.
In our board, voltage is the positive output terminal voltage, and current is
the positive current delivered to the load.
Under fixed illumination, current is greatest near the short circuit end and
falls to zero at the open circuit voltage.
At short circuit the terminal voltage is zero, so useful terminal power V I is
zero despite the current.
At open circuit the current is zero, so terminal power is also zero despite
the voltage.
The useful operating point lies between these extremes.
Suppose the cell supplies zero point five volts and twenty milliamperes to a
load.
Multiply zero point five by zero point zero two amperes.
Output power is zero point zero one watt, or ten milliwatts.
If fifty milliwatts of optical power fall on the active area, the efficiency
at
that operating point is ten divided by fifty, or twenty percent.
That is an assumed example, not a promise about every solar cell.
Maximum power operation depends on the I V curve, illumination, and
temperature.
For JEE, do not confuse open circuit voltage with maximum power, or short
circuit current with a useful power output.
Our ordinary diode lesson treated reverse breakdown as a condition to avoid
unless the device is designed for it.
A Zener diode is designed for controlled reverse breakdown operation within
its
ratings.
Connect it reverse biased and limit the current.
Once its reverse voltage reaches the operating region around V Z, current can
change substantially while voltage changes relatively little.
On the usual signed diode I V graph, reverse voltage and reverse current
appear
on the negative sides.
The labels V Z and I Z in our numerical examples are positive magnitudes.
That avoids accidentally reporting negative power.
The curve is not a perfectly vertical line: real devices have a finite slope
resistance and a useful current range.
Also, the microscopic mechanism can involve Zener tunneling, avalanche
processes, or both, depending on the device.
You do not need to label every breakdown event as one identical process.
For a five point one volt Zener carrying ten milliamperes in reverse, power is
five point one times zero point zero one, or zero point zero five one watts.
That is fifty one milliwatts.
Compare this with the power rating and the allowed operating current.
A series resistor is not optional in the simple supply circuit; it prevents
excessive current.
Pause and distinguish polarity from magnitude.
The Zener is reverse biased, but its dissipated power is positive.
Regulation requires a suitable current, not just writing the breakdown voltage
next to an unloaded diode.
Let's solve a complete regulator example, because the current split is where
JEE questions become interesting.
A twelve volt source feeds a three hundred thirty ohm series resistor.
A five point one volt Zener is reverse connected across a five hundred ten ohm
load.
Assume the Zener's specified useful current range for this exercise is five to
thirty milliamperes.
If it regulates, the series resistor drops twelve minus five point one, or six
point nine volts.
Divide by three hundred thirty: source current is about twenty point nine one
milliamperes.
Load current is five point one divided by five hundred ten, or ten
milliamperes.
The remaining ten point nine one milliamperes flows through the Zener.
It is inside the assumed current range, and Zener power is about fifty five
point six milliwatts.
Now change the load resistance to one hundred seventy ohms.
If voltage stayed at five point one, load current would be thirty
milliamperes,
more than the resistor can supply.
Subtracting gives a negative assumed Zener current.
That is a warning that our regulating model is inconsistent, not a real
negative breakdown current.
In the simple off Zener approximation, the circuit becomes a divider: output
is
twelve times one hundred seventy divided by five hundred, or four point zero
eight volts, below breakdown.
Think before trusting V Z as the output.
Always test the current balance and ratings.
A regulator maintains voltage only within its operating conditions, not for
every supply and every load.
